The Sleek lates (Lates stappersii) is a large centropomid predator endemic to Lake Tanganyika, where it occupies the pelagic zone and feeds primarily on small schooling fishes. Field surveys and captive rearing studies have provided valuable insights into its growth trajectory, with individuals attaining a maximum recorded total length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters]. This ultimate length places the species among the larger members of its genus, though it remains considerably smaller than the closely related Nile perch. The size at which gonadal development begins has been documented through histological examination of wild-caught specimens; puberty, defined by the onset of spermatogenesis or vitellogenesis in the gonads, is consistently observed at a standard length of 23.6 centimeters [Lp = 23.6 centimeters]. This relatively early maturation relative to ultimate size may reflect an adaptive response to the high mortality pressures typical of pelagic predators in the Tanganyikan system, where early reproductive onset can offset substantial losses during the larval and juvenile stages.

Egg production and spawning frequency in Sleek lates have been examined using captive broodstock maintained under controlled thermal conditions. At a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], females produce a maximum of approximately 67000 eggs across the entire annual spawning season [Ri = approximately 67000 eggs across the entire annual spawning season], though this output is distributed across multiple spawning events rather than released in a single clutch. The high fecundity is characteristic of pelagic spawners that produce small, buoyant eggs with minimal parental investment, and it aligns closely with values reported for the striped trumpeter (Latris lineata) when scaled for body size. The same thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] also governs the duration of embryonic development: freshly fertilized eggs hatch after just 8 days [ab = 8 days], a relatively rapid incubation period that is typical of tropical freshwater teleosts and likely reduces the window of vulnerability to benthic egg predators.

Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae of Sleek lates are notably small, reflecting the modest egg diameter of this species. Measurements taken from captive-reared cohorts indicate that the wet weight at birth averages approximately 0.0012 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0012 grams], a value that is consistent with the egg diameter of roughly 1.3 millimeters observed in the striped trumpeter and other latids. This minute initial mass imposes a critical constraint on early larval survival: the yolk reserves must sustain the prolarva until the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding can be initiated, a period during which starvation risk is high. The larval period is marked by rapid somatic growth fueled by intensive feeding on zooplankton, and individuals that survive the initial bottleneck eventually undergo a pelagic-benthic transition as they recruit to juvenile habitats in the littoral zone.

As Sleek lates approaches its asymptotic size, the ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults has been estimated from length-weight regressions based on extensive sampling of the commercial fishery. The maximum body mass recorded for this species is 713 grams [Wwi = 713 grams], a value derived from the allometric relationship 0.00813 times total length raised to the power of 2.99, which indicates a slightly negatively allometric growth pattern relative to a pure isometric cube law. This relatively modest adult mass, coupled with a standard length at first reproduction of 23.6 centimeters [Lp = 23.6 centimeters], suggests a life history strategy that prioritizes early maturation and high fecundity over the attainment of extreme body size. Such traits are characteristic of pelagic, schooling fishes that face size-independent predation throughout much of their adult lives.

Longevity data for Sleek lates, drawn from mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age determinations, indicate that the maximum lifespan in the wild under the baseline thermal conditions of the lake (approximately 25 °C [T = 25 °C]) is roughly 33 years [am = roughly 33 years]. This considerable lifespan is noteworthy for a fish of its size and suggests that once individuals reach reproductive maturity, adult mortality rates are relatively low, possibly due to the paucity of large piscivores in the Tanganyikan pelagic zone. The combination of an age at hatching of only 8 days [ab = 8 days] under the same thermal conditions and a lifespan extending over three decades places the species at the slow end of the fast-slow continuum for tropical fishes at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. Such extended longevity may facilitate multiple reproductive bouts across the life cycle, consistent with the iteroparous spawning strategy inferred from the sustained annual fecundity of 67000 eggs per year [Ri = 67000 eggs per year] recorded in the captive broodstock.
